text:
Sampled cross-entropy (CE) makes candidates compete through one denominator; BPR compares positive–negative pairs independently; BCE classifies each score independently. CE with exactly one negative equals BPR at matched logits/temperature ([theoretical analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770)). Direct differentiation: for scores s/τ, CE gradients are (p_positive−1)/τ and p_negative/τ, concentrating negative pressure on high-scoring candidates. Increasing K changes competition and hard-negative coverage, not simply gradient scale. Lower τ sharpens competition and introduces a 1/τ factor, but saturation means gradient magnitude need not increase monotonically. Temperature also interacts with embedding normalization and learned norms ([sampled-softmax study](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf)). Positive inference-time temperature scaling alone preserves ranking.

Reduction is a major confound. Summed K-negative BPR has K times the gradient of its pairwise mean on identical samples. BCE positive-plus-summed-negatives changes class balance as K grows; averaging all K+1 terms also shrinks the positive coefficient. Positive-plus-mean-negatives preserves explicit class weights. These are algebraic consequences, not evidence that one objective wins. Sequential-recommendation experiments confirm loss and negative count can substantially affect apparent architecture gains ([authors’ experiments](https://github.com/antklen/sasrec-bert4rec-recsys23)).

Controlled ablations: retain the supplied BERT4Rec backbone, masked targets, appended-mask inference, seeds, splits and training limits. First compare objectives using identical negative draws, K, temperature, score normalization and target weights; K=1 CE/BPR provides an equivalence check. Then vary K alone, reduction alone, and τ alone; separately test explicit terminal-target weighting. Record terminal/interior gradient norms, clipping frequency, score margins, embedding norms, runtime and macro validation HR@10. Scalar loss matching cannot remove candidate-dependent weighting; Adam and clipping complicate learning-rate compensation. Train one model per category; take exact baseline settings from the host.
